name: Wasembo
confidence_why: Jones 2025, the only first-hand description that states a rule, gives penultimate primary stress with its exceptions explained as univerbation, while the McElhanon & Sogum 1976 wordlist marks stress without stating a rule and shows disyllables uniformly penultimate but several trisyllables (námbehe, yóhoma, nínira, hépera) with initial stress, so the record rests on one modern source with only minor tension from an older one-session elicitation.

catalog_quote: Hurukui (ISO 639-3: [gsp]; also known as Wasembo) belongs to the Rai Coast subgroup of the Madang branch of Trans-New Guinea (Z‘graggen 1975, Pawley & Hammarström 2018). ... [2.1 Relevant phonology] There are two types of stress in Hurukui: primary and secondary. Primary stress is realized as high pitch, increased length, and greater intensity. Secondary stress is realized as increased length and greater intensity, but without high pitch. Hurukui normally assigns stress to the penultimate syllable of a word, and normally assigns a single primary stress and no secondary stresses. I consider exceptions to this as evidence that a sequence of more than one word has become, or is becoming, one. Secondary stress is found in words that have been created by univerbation, occurring wherever primary stress used to be in a sequence of morphemes that has lost its ability to carry primary stress. In the orthography used in this paper, I mark irregularly placed primary stress with acute accent, and I mark secondary stress with grave accent.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: In the notation primary stress is indicated by the acute accent (´) and secondary stress by the grave accent (`). Primary stress is accompanied by the highest tone of the word. The symbol r represents an alveolar flap.
new_statements.citation: McElhanon, Kenneth A. & Sigkepe Sogum. 1976. English-Wasembo vocabulary. In Richard Loving (ed.), Surveys in five Papua New Guinea languages (Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 16), 113-119. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics.
new_statements.locator: p. 113, second introductory paragraph (immediately before the wordlist)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Rendered p. 1 (printed p. 113) of at 150 dpi and read the page scan. The second introductory paragraph reads exactly: "In the notation primary stress is indicated by the acute accent (') and secondary stress by the grave accent (`). Primary stress is accompanied by the highest tone of the word. The symbol r represents an alveolar flap." (r underlined in print). Verbatim match; the. renders the two accent glyphs as (*) and (‘) but the image is unambiguous. The passage is preceded by the recording note (31 October 1973, elicited via Kâte, Sogum the consultant, "high degree of accuracy") and followed by the Pihom/Rai Coast classification paragraph, as the compiler describes. No placemen…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The source states that Wasembo has primary and secondary word stress and that the primary-stressed syllable carries the word's highest pitch, but it gives no placement rule; stress is simply marked on every entry. Reading the marked forms on pp. 114-115 (from the page scan): disyllables are mostly initial (kʰúha 'all', mása 'bad', mónu 'bird', kíma 'blunt', gúnu 'dam', máha 'dust') but bound verb/noun roots often end-stressed (hipá- 'anus', ekʰá- 'to dance', umé- 'to die', ipó- 'father', hoká- 'to cut'); trisyllables split between initial (námbehe 'banana', yóhoma 'bird of paradise', nínira 'black', hépera 'borer', námbiŋgi 'cassowary', mísiku 'childless', úteme 'fireplace', kákumu 'dust', wámbora 'floor') and second-syllable (kʰarána 'adze', itéme 'ashes', itépa 'bandicoot', awéhe 'blossom', naŋgóra 'cabbage', gobóre 'cloud', pukʰáne 'breadfruit', kiŋgáye 'blue', hoŋgáhi 'firefly', goráane 'egg'); so primary stress falls on the first or second syllable with no rule stated and no obvious segmental conditioning, hence the provisional 'lexical' reading. An alternative hypothesis the data would allow is weight-sensitivity (stressed long vowels in goráane, yaŋgáapu, akáaka), untested.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Marked with the grave accent. In four-syllable words it falls two syllables after an initial primary: émekàra 'between', úmbugùra 'cold', háwiràyo 'centipede', hónoŋgàri 'earthworm', mámaŋgàri 'fly', húŋgumugì- 'armpit', kúŋguŋgè- 'to dry'; also on a final root syllable after initial primary in pókʰonà- 'back', gébanè- 'chest', mágagè- 'chin', wákʰupʰè- 'blood'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; variant pairs such as omá-/óma- 'arm' and yóhɔ/yóho/uráho 'fire' show alternative stressings for the same gloss.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms in an elicited English-Wasembo wordlist (recorded 31 Oct 1973 through Kâte as the contact language, 'high degree of accuracy' claimed by the authors); nouns given with possessive-suffix hyphen and verbs as bound roots with hyphen, so the stress marks are on stems, not full inflected words. 'Highest tone of the word' means the stressed syllable carries the pitch peak; no tonal contrast is claimed.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1976 vocabulary and the 1975 sketch both name the language Wasembo (or Gusap), spoken in the five villages Gusap, Hinggia, Yankowan, Rampa and Maraboi east of the Gusap aerodrome, Markham headwaters, Morobe Province: this is wase1252 (Glottolog alternative names Gusap, Yankowan, Biapim). Jones 2023 calls the same language Horokoi (hh.bib: 'Horokoi = Wasembo [gsp]'). The wordlist data come from a single speaker, Sigkepe Sogum, village not stated.

readall_conflicts: The pre-existing tension stays as it was: the catalog rule (penultimate stress = penultimate, src world-r2-2026-09-17) rests on Jones 2025 (already held by the project from the earlier stage: lines 542-544, ms. p. 11 Section 2.1: 'Hurukui normally assigns stress to the penultimate syllable of a word, and normally assigns a single primary stress and no secondary stresses'), whereas the existing_statement from McElhanon & Sogum 1976 (p. 113) only defines the acute/grave notation and says primary stress carries the highest tone of the word, without stating a placement rule, which is why it was read as lexical/unpredictable. These are compatible rather than contradictory: a wordlist that marks stress on every entry need not imply unpredictability, and Jones gives an explicit penultimate default with marked exceptions (serial-verb forms with final stress, 1SG.FUT with antepenultimate stress, secondary stress only in univerbated sequences).
